videos.description:
One day the bug was literal. Engineers had called faults bugs since Edison. On this one afternoon, someone opened a relay and found an actual insect.

9 September. An operator traced a fault to a moth caught in a relay, removed it, and taped it into the log book instead of throwing it away.

First actual case of bug being found. Relay #70, Panel F. 15:45. The wording gives it away, they knew the joke they were making.

They kept the moth.

In 1975 it turned up in Businessweek. In a feature called The Office of the Future. The idea was worth reporting before it was furniture.

videos.title: Atari buried its games in the desert.
videos.description:
Atari buried its games in the desert. September 1983: trucks took hundreds of thousands of cartridges out to a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, and buried them.

The New York Times reported it at the time. Then it slid out of the record and became a story gamers told each other, always about E.T.

All of it was true. The city, archaeologists and a film crew went ten metres down and pulled up just over 1,300 cartridges. Not only E.T.

The Smithsonian took some. So did the Henry Ford, the Strong Museum of Play and the video game museum in Rome. A landfill became a catalogued site.

The urban legend had a manifest.

videos.title: You have never once questioned this.
videos.description:
You have never once questioned this.

It was built to slow you down. So the typebars would not jam. It is in textbooks. The researchers who traced the layout's real history called that, in print, nonsense.

At Kyoto University they followed the keyboard back past the typewriter to the telegraph. Its first heavy users were Morse operators taking down code live.

American Morse writes Z almost like S-E. An operator could not tell them apart until the following letters arrived. So S ended up next to both Z and E.

Sholes spent his last year trying to replace it.

Was pollinated by hand. The orchid has its own bee only in Mexico. Everywhere else someone opens each flower and does it themselves, one at a time.

Twelve, born into slavery on Réunion and taught horticulture by the man who owned him. He saw the flower's two halves were separated by a flap you could lift.

Then more pods appeared. Bellier-Beaumont had kept one barren vine alive twenty years. In 1861 he wrote that the boy worked it out himself.

He said he taught the boy. Bellier-Beaumont checked the dates: by that account Edmond was eight. Archivists went back over it in 2009 and agreed it was his.

He died in a public hospital with nothing.

videos.title: The three-finger salute.
videos.description:
The three-finger salute.

It was a private developer tool. Rebooting IBM's prototype PC meant sitting through memory tests on every restart. The team hunting bugs rebooted every five minutes. One of them got tired of waiting.

The 12th of 12 engineers on the secret PC project in Boca Raton. His instant-reboot shortcut took five or ten minutes, one item on a list of a hundred tasks.

One hand cannot press them. Del sat across the keyboard from Ctrl and Alt, so no accident could trigger it. The public only found out because IBM printed it in the technical manual.

I may have invented it, but Bill made it famous.

videos.title: Is there coffee, or not.
videos.description:
Is there coffee, or not. Cambridge's Computer Laboratory had seven floors and one filter machine. In 1991, researchers pointed a camera at it so nobody climbed the stairs to an empty pot.

One wrote the client, XCoffee, and the other the server, feeding a 128-by-128 greyscale image of the pot to every desk on the lab network.

The pot joined the web. Browsers had just learned to display images. Daniel Gordon and Martyn Johnson put the feed on a page, and the lab's coffee became visible worldwide.

They switched it off. The shutdown made the front pages of The Times and The Washington Post. The last pot went to eBay, where Der Spiegel paid £3,350 for it.

A webcam now points at it, in a museum.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Room_coffee_pot
- https://quentinsf.com/coffeepot/

videos.title: It was all demoed at once.
videos.description:
It was all demoed at once. The mouse, windows, hypertext, video calls, live shared editing, shown working together in San Francisco in 1968, before any of it was a product.

9 December, a 90-minute session at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. He sat alone on stage under the lights, driving a computer the audience could not see.

The computer was in Menlo Park, that far away. A homemade 2,400-baud modem carried his keystrokes; microwave dishes beamed the video back.

The cord looked like a tail. Bill English built the first mouse in 1964 from Engelbart's sketches: a wooden shell, two metal wheels, one button. On stage, Engelbart admitted nobody remembered who named it.

He remembered the crowd standing, cheering like crazy.

- https://invention.si.edu/invention-stories/mother-all-demos

videos.title: It was an average, at one music school.
videos.description:
It was an average, at one music school. Violinists in Berlin, sorted by how good their teachers thought they were. By age twenty the best group averaged over 10,000 hours, the good group about 7,800, the least accomplished about 4,600. A gradient, not a gate.

Outliers turned that gradient into the ten-thousand-hour rule, the idea that ten thousand hours of practice makes an expert. The 1993 paper it came from does not say so anywhere.

They were remembered. Each musician was asked to estimate how much they had practised per week, for every year of their life, looking backwards. Every hour in the study is a recollection of an hour.

In a 2014 meta-analysis, that is all the variance in performance deliberate practice explained, once you restrict it to the studies that logged practice as it happened instead of asking people to recall it.

The number moves with the room. Practice explained 26 percent of the variance in games, 21 in music, 18 in sports, 4 in education, and under 1 percent in the professions. Their own summary: important, but not as important as has been argued.

Sources:
- https://scottbarrykaufman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Macnamara-et-al.-2014.pdf

videos.title: It snowed in June.
videos.description:
It snowed in June. May frost killed the crops across New England. June snow fell on Albany. In July there was still ice on Pennsylvania rivers.

videos.title: Wi-Fi is short for Wireless Fidelity.
videos.description:
Wi-Fi is short for Wireless Fidelity. The dictionary calls that reading spurious. Phil Belanger, who ran the naming, is blunter: it is not an acronym, and there is no meaning.

The alliance behind the new 802.11b radio could not market "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence," so it hired the agency that had named Prozac and Compaq. What came back was Wi-Fi, a pun on hi-fi, chosen from a list of ten.

The name was chosen first. The meaning was bolted on. Some board members could not stomach a name that explained nothing, so they added the tag line "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity." It ran about a year, then was quietly retired.

The group never wrote a standard. It certifies that devices interoperate; the standard is IEEE's. So the phrase is wrong on both words, Belanger's own verdict is that it only diluted the brand.

The man who picked the name spent years asking people to forget the tag line.

The story says it is named after a room at CERN. The legend: room 404 held the web's first server, or Tim Berners-Lee's office, and anything the server could not locate was 'not found in room 404'. It is told constantly. It is also wrong.

The 4 means you erred. The rest just means 'not found'. In HTTP every reply carries a status code. Codes starting with 4 mean the client made the mistake, a bad or missing request. 404 sits with 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden. Nothing more.

Wrote the codes into the young web's specification at CERN. The definition has read the same ever since: 'The server has not found anything matching the URI given.' A slot in a table, not a door.

There was never a room 404 at CERN. There is only the list, and the fourth kind of error on it.

Nintendo has stolen King Kong, they say. Universal claimed Donkey Kong infringed its King Kong trademark. Awkwardly, seven years earlier Universal had gone to court to argue the opposite: that the King Kong story belonged to no one, and was in the public domain.

videos.title: The story says it is named after a room at CERN.
videos.description:
The story says it is named after a room at CERN. The legend: room 404 held the web's first server, or Tim Berners-Lee's office, and anything the server could not locate was 'not found in room 404'. It is told constantly. It is also wrong.

The 4 means you erred. The rest just means 'not found'. In HTTP every reply carries a status code. Codes starting with 4 mean the client made the mistake, a bad or missing request. 404 sits with 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden. Nothing more.

Wrote the codes into the young web's specification at CERN. The definition has read the same ever since: 'The server has not found anything matching the URI given.' A slot in a table, not a door.

There was never a room 404 at CERN. There is only the list, and the fourth kind of error on it.

Sources:
- https://www.w3.org/Protocols/HTTP/HTRESP.html (W3C, 'Status codes in HTTP', a historic CERN and W3C document dated 1992; read in full 27 August 2026): established that HTTP groups its status codes by leading digit, that the '4xx codes are intended for cases in which the client seems to have erred' while 5xx codes are for server errors, and that 404 is defined as 'Not found: The server has not found anything matching the URI given', listed alongside 400 Bad request, 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden.

videos.title: On Venus it is literally true.
videos.description:
On Venus it is literally true. Venus takes 243 Earth days to turn once on its axis, and only 225 to circle the Sun. Complete a single rotation and you have already outlived a Venus year, with eighteen days to spare.

One rotation of Venus, in Earth days, the slowest spin of any planet in the Solar System. Its whole year is shorter, at 225.

On Venus the Sun rises in the west. Venus spins backwards compared with Earth and nearly every other planet. Sunrise to sunset, if you could see the Sun through the acid cloud, takes about 117 Earth days.

Venus's clouds hid its spin for centuries. Astronomers could time only the cloud tops, which race round in about four days. When radar first reached the surface in 1962, it revealed that the planet beneath barely turns at all.

Florida feminist who founded the United States' first rape treatment centre and led the campaign to end female-only hurricane names, arguing that women 'deeply resent being arbitrarily associated with disaster'.

videos.title: Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old.
videos.description:
Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old. Ancient Egyptian tombs in particular have turned up jars of honey that are millennia old and, once opened, still edible.

Raw nectar is mostly water. Finished honey barely is. Bees fan the nectar with their wings until most of the moisture is gone, leaving too little water for bacteria to get a foothold.

Honey is acidic, and it makes its own disinfectant. A pH of roughly 3 to 4.5 already kills off most microbes. An enzyme from the bees' own stomachs adds hydrogen peroxide on top, the same compound used to clean wounds.

Honey has been medicine for thousands of years. The earliest written use is on Sumerian clay tablets, where honey appears in roughly three in ten prescriptions. Egyptian physicians used it as a wound and eye ointment, because nothing could grow on it long enough to cause an infection.

It only works sealed. Crack the jar and let the damp in, and even honey can finally spoil.

Established that archaeologists have repeatedly found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old and still preserved; that honey is hygroscopic and bees actively dry the nectar, which starts at 60 to 80 per cent water, by flapping their wings, leaving too little moisture for microbes to survive; that honey's pH sits at roughly 3 to 4.5, acidic enough to kill off almost anything trying to grow in it; that bees carry an enzyme, glucose oxidase, which mixes with the nectar during regurgitation into the comb and produces gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, adding further antimicrobial power; that the earliest recorded medicinal use of honey is on Sumerian clay tablets, where it appears in roughly 30 per cent of prescriptions, and that ancient Egyptian physicians used honey ointments on skin and eye conditions because nothing could grow on an open wound covered in it; and that the preservation holds only while the jar stays sealed, since added water or an open lid can let it spoil after all.

videos.title: You start seeing the blocks with your eyes shut.
videos.description:
You start seeing the blocks with your eyes shut. Falling, turning, slotting into gaps, right at the edge of sleep. Harvard researchers put numbers on it in 2000: 17 of 27 players reported the same images.

His team trained volunteers on Tetris for three days and woke them at sleep onset. The reports were eerily alike: everyone saw pieces falling, nobody saw the score, the board, or the keyboard.

Amnesiacs saw the blocks too, with no memory of the game. Five patients with hippocampal damage could not recall playing. Three still saw falling pieces as they dozed. One sat down and set her fingers on the right keys, not knowing why.

The dream came without the memory that should carry it. The pictures surfaced even when the conscious record of the day was gone: evidence that sleep-onset imagery runs on a different memory system than the one that recalls events.

The players who needed to learn the most were the ones who dreamed of it most.

videos.title: It started as one economist's footnote about dirt.
videos.description:
It started as one economist's footnote about dirt. In 1896, Vilfredo Pareto noticed that roughly 80 percent of the land in Italy belonged to about 20 percent of the population. That's the whole original observation.

A different man did that, four decades later. In 1941, engineer Joseph Juran read Pareto's land-ownership statistic and did something Pareto never did: he claimed it was universal, true of defects, sales and complaints, almost anything you can count.

An engineer working in quality control. He renamed Pareto's one-off Italian statistic 'the vital few and the useful many,' and spent the following six decades teaching that it applied to almost everything.

Juran's age when he died in 2008, having outlived the man he named the principle after by more than eighty years, and taught the idea the whole time.

Pareto counted Italian land. Juran turned it into a rule for everything.

Juran, having read Pareto's work, generalised the observation and later named it 'the vital few and the useful many'; cites Juran's New York Times obituary (Bunkley, 3 March 2008) for his death at age 103.

videos.title: Parkinson admitted upfront that story was made up.
videos.description:
Parkinson admitted upfront that story was made up. The real piece was a satirical nine-page article for The Economist in November 1955, and it's still quoted today as if it were a study.

Officials up 78 percent, while the fleet shrank by two-thirds. It reads like scientific proof. Parkinson never disclosed where the numbers came from.

The true growth was even bigger than Parkinson said, and so was the reason he left out. The honest 1914 baseline was lower, pushing the real increase closer to 120 percent. That surge tracks almost exactly with the paperwork of the First World War, which Parkinson's essay never mentions once.

A serious naval historian, Raffles Professor of History at the University of Malaya, in Singapore, whose nine-page joke in The Economist was collected into a book that sold nearly a quarter of a million copies in two years.

Historian Jon Sumida's corrected 1914-to-1928 growth rate, using the actual Navy Lists rather than Parkinson's undisclosed source.

videos.title: A schoolboy watched his hot ice-cream mix freeze before the cold batch.
videos.description:
A schoolboy watched his hot ice-cream mix freeze before the cold batch. Erasto Mpemba was in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School. His teacher told him that was simply not possible.

"Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun." Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes both noted it too, centuries before Mpemba was born. None of that stopped it from being named after him.

A physicist who met Mpemba at his next school, tested the claim with water back in his own lab, and confirmed it. They published together in Physics Education under the title "Cool?", while Mpemba was training at the College of African Wildlife Management, not a physics department.

In 2016, two researchers finally tested it under tightly controlled conditions. Henry Burridge and Paul Linden's own conclusion: "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect."

It's still taught as settled science in classrooms that have never settled it.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba_effect: read in full. Establishes: Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian student, noticed in 1963 in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School (Tanganyika) that a hot ice-cream mixture froze before a cold one in cookery class, and his teacher dismissed it; he later raised it with visiting physicist Denis Osborne at Mkwawa Secondary School; Osborne tested it with water at his own workplace and confirmed it; they co-published "Cool?" in Physics Education 4(3):172-175 in 1969, while Mpemba was studying at the College of African Wildlife Management; Aristotle wrote centuries earlier, "Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun"; Francis Bacon separately noted "slightly tepid water freezes more easily than that which is utterly cold"; Rene Descartes described the same pattern in his Discourse on the Method; in 2016, Henry Burridge and Paul Linden tested the time water takes to reach 0°C under tightly controlled conditions and concluded, in their own words, "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect"; the article states physicists remain divided on the effect's reproducibility, precise definition and underlying mechanism.

videos.title: No study ever found that number.
videos.description:
No study ever found that number. The claim that goldfish forget everything after three seconds, sometimes told as seven, has no traceable scientific source. It just got repeated until it sounded like one.

Goldfish have a region built for spatial memory. It sits in roughly the same place the hippocampus does in a human brain, the part used for remembering routes and layouts, not for forgetting them in seconds.

At the University of Hawaii, paired a light with a mild shock in goldfish and varied the gap between them. The fear response behaved exactly as Pavlov's conditioning model predicted, evidence of a learned association, not just a reflex.

The goldfish still finds the food. In a maze-training study recognised by the American Museum of Natural History, a goldfish that learned a route to a food reward reached it again, adjusting its path, after the maze was rotated 180 degrees.

The fish everyone mocks for forgetting has been quietly passing memory tests since the 1960s.

videos.title: The speed-up is an accident.
videos.description:
The speed-up is an accident. In Space Invaders the aliens surge faster as you shoot them down. Nothing in the game's code speeds them up. Open the original ROM and that instruction simply isn't there.

Built the whole game almost single-handed for Taito, running on an Intel 8080. With 55 aliens to move, redraw and test for hits, the chip could barely keep pace.

Every one is a sprite the processor must shift, draw and check each frame. At the start of a wave, all that work drags the whole screen slow.

Fewer aliens, faster frame. Each kill leaves the 8080 less to compute, so the survivors accelerate. The famous rising panic is the hardware exhaling, not a difficulty curve someone drew.

The best mechanic in the game is a bug nobody wrote.

Sources:
- https://www.tomshardware.com/video-games/retro-gaming/space-invaders-arcade-game-ran-faster-as-enemies-died-due-to-intel-8080-bottleneck-expert-coder-asserts-hardware-accident-to-blame: Tom's Hardware (26 Oct 2025), read directly: Space Invaders was launched by Taito in Japan in June 1978 on an Intel 8080 (launched 1974, ~2 MHz); a code analysis of the original ROM shows there is NO instruction that adjusts game speed as aliens die; the acceleration is a hardware side-effect: with 55 aliens to reposition, redraw and collision-check the 8080 runs slowly, and each alien destroyed frees the processor so the survivors move faster.

videos.description:
It started as a side effect. Street Fighter II, 1991. The chained hits that built the whole genre were never designed. They fell out of a system built to do something else.

Press a special too fast and it still came out. Input leniency, added so a rushed motion would not swallow your fireball. The side effect: you could cancel a normal attack straight into a special.

Lead designer. On the cancel: "It didn't seem to cause any bugs, so we decided it could be a feature to expand the gameplay." They left it in, sure most players would never land it.

"Since we decided to incorporate it, I wouldn't call it a bug."

"Combo" arrived two years late. Super Street Fighter II, in 1993, added the on-screen combo counter. The mechanic itself shipped in 1991 with no name, no counter and no plan for it.

videos.title: They were never chasing you at random.
videos.description:
They were never chasing you at random. Each of the four ghosts runs its own fixed formula for picking a target tile, results Namco's own team called their "personalities".

Pinky isn't chasing you. He's ambushing you. His target sits four tiles ahead of wherever you're currently facing, so he tries to cut off your path instead of following it.

Face upward, and the maths breaks. A logic error in the original code adds a phantom four-tile offset to the left as well, so "four tiles up" becomes four up and four left. It shipped in 1980 and stayed.

The programmer Namco paired with designer Toru Iwatani, who had no formal coding background himself. Between them they built four different hunting formulas, not four costumes on one script.

Clyde's actual personal-space rule. Closer than this and he panics back to his corner; farther and he hunts you exactly like the red ghost.

videos.title: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom.
videos.description:
Old church windows are thicker at the bottom. The story goes that over 800 years the glass crept downward under its own weight. It is the most repeated fact about glass, and it is false.

You would wait out the universe, and then some. Physicists estimate the flow would take around a hundred thousand billion billion years. The universe is under fourteen billion years old. Medieval glass has not had a rounding error of the time it would need.

They were made that way, then stood that way up. Medieval glass was blown into cylinders, split and flattened by hand, so no sheet came out even. Glaziers simply set the thick edge at the bottom. The 'flow' is a fitter's choice, held for 800 years.

Glass is not quite a solid either. It is its own state, on a clock nobody will ever read out.

Sources:
- https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/glass-transition/myth.php (University of Cambridge DoITPoMS, 'Do Cathedral Glasses Flow?'; read in full 26 Aug 2026): establishes the myth that over centuries cathedral window glass flows downward under gravity, leaving panes thicker at the bottom; that Zanotto and Gupta calculated the room-temperature relaxation time for such flow at about ten to the power of 23 years, far beyond the age of the Universe at about ten to the power of 10 years; and the real cause, that medieval glass was blown into large cylinders which were split and flattened by hand so it was never of even thickness, with fitters instinctively placing the thicker edge at the bottom. Cites E.D. Zanotto, 'Do cathedral glasses flow?', American Journal of Physics 66, 392-395 (1998).
- https://www.livescience.com/chemistry/is-glass-a-liquid-or-a-solid (Live Science, Victoria Atkinson, 24 Sep 2023; read in full 26 Aug 2026): materials scientist John Mauro of Penn State says glass is neither a true liquid nor a true solid but its own distinct, nonequilibrium, noncrystalline state that appears solid on short timescales and relaxes towards a liquid only over billions of years; John Parker of the Sheffield Centre for Glass Research says that in a practical sense glass is a rigid solid on any sensible timescale, and that the old panes are thicker at the bottom because a thousand years ago makers could not produce glass of uniform thickness.

"There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." It's credited to one man, Phil Karlton, and nobody has ever produced anything he wrote it in.

He couldn't find one either. In a 2017 post, David Karlton collected every citation of the quote he could find online and admitted none of them traced back further than secondhand memory.

Engineer at Xerox PARC, DEC, Silicon Graphics and Netscape, where he helped build X Windows and an internet security protocol. Killed in a car accident near Canelli, Italy, that June, at 50, taking the actual origin of his own line with him.

He recalls hearing it at Carnegie Mellon, around 1970. Karlton really did study there, years before his Xerox and Netscape career, but the memory is one blog comment, not a document, so the earliest confirmed instance of his own line is still unknown.

The internet gave it a third hard thing anyway: off-by-one errors.

videos.title: "CAPTCHA" was coined in 2003. The test already existed.
videos.description:
"CAPTCHA" was coined in 2003. The test already existed. Distorted-letter tests to block bots were already live in 2000, when idrive.com started using one, and PayPal adopted the same idea in 2001, years before anyone called it a CAPTCHA.

It stands for something nobody would say out loud. Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. Von Ahn, Blum, Hopper and Langford built the acronym to fit the word, not the other way round.

Carnegie Mellon researcher who turned the same idea into reCAPTCHA: instead of random letters, it showed real words that book-scanning software could not read, so solving the puzzle also helped digitise old text.

Google bought it in 2009. The Carnegie Mellon spin-off was acquired within a year of being founded, and reCAPTCHA went on to help digitise The New York Times' archive and Google Books.

A test built to prove you're not a computer. A 2018 study trained one to pass it using 500 examples.

Most answers land on Pong, 1972. A playable video game had already drawn crowds about fourteen years earlier, at a nuclear lab's open house, on an oscilloscope the size of a saucer.

A physicist who built radar displays at MIT and timing circuits for the first atomic bomb. To liven up Brookhaven Lab's dull visitors' day he wired a tennis game onto an analog computer, taking the ball's arc straight from a bouncing-ball example in the machine's manual.

He never filed a patent. He already held twenty; this one seemed no more novel than the manual's circuit. And at a government lab, any patent would have belonged to Washington, not to him.

A cathode-ray amusement device was patented in 1948. Goldsmith and Mann's tube let you fire at targets, but you taped paper planes over the glass, because it could not draw them. Higinbotham's court, net and ball were all on the screen.

videos.title: People supposedly work harder simply because they know they are being watched.
videos.description:
People supposedly work harder simply because they know they are being watched. That lesson comes from a 1920s factory study. There is a problem: the economists who finally found the original data were not convinced it happened as taught.

Coined the term 'Hawthorne effect', nearly three decades after the studies it describes had ended. The name was applied retrospectively to results nobody had cleanly explained at the time.

Output rose in the room where nothing changed too. Researchers dimmed and brightened the lights in one room while leaving a second, unlit control room alone. Productivity climbed in both, which meant the lighting was never the real variable.

How long the original 1924 lighting data sat unexamined, until economists Steven Levitt and John List found it on microfilm in 2011 and reported only weak support for the effect nearly everyone had been taught.

'A glorified anecdote.' Richard Nisbett's verdict on the whole idea: 'Once you have got the anecdote, you can throw away the data.'

was drawn for a cartoon dog. Comic Sans exists because of Rover, the animated dog in Microsoft Bob, a mid-90s program meant to make the PC friendly for beginners.

A Microsoft designer. He opened a beta of Bob and found the dog speaking through a Times New Roman speech bubble. 'Dogs don't talk in Times New Roman,' he said, and started drawing.

not any real handwriting. Connare modelled the letters on the hand-lettering in graphic novels sitting on his desk, a casual voice for a cartoon, never meant for résumés or wedding invitations.

The font built for the dog never made it into the dog's program.

videos.title: It was a merchant's mark, centuries before email.
videos.description:
It was a merchant's mark, centuries before email. It meant 'at the rate of': three crates @ two shillings. A trader's shorthand for a price, not a piece of computer punctuation.

A Florentine merchant wrote the earliest known @ (standing in for an amphora, a unit of wine) in a letter about treasure the conquistadors shipped from Peru. In Spanish and Portuguese the sign is still 'arroba,' a unit of weight.

@ had sat on typewriter keyboards since the 1880s. Little used, always there. Which is exactly why it was free for the taking when networks needed a character that would never turn up inside someone's name.

Ray Tomlinson grabbed @ to split the name from the machine. It was not an assignment: he was fooling around with ARPANET. He needed one symbol to mean this user at this computer, and @ already meant at. The address bar has looked that way ever since.

A mark for pricing wine now sits in New York's Museum of Modern Art, credited to Tomlinson.

Sources:
- https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/104059-first-instance-of-at-sign: Guinness World Records, read in full. Establishes: per history professor Giorgio Stabile (La Sapienza, Rome), the first documented, credible appearance of @ dates to 4 May 1536, when Italian merchant Francesco Lapi used it to stand for an amphora (a unit of measurement) in a letter about treasure shipped by the conquistadors from Peru; earlier medieval-scribe uses arguably exist, but Lapi's is the first known use of @ as a character with a distinct meaning; an amphora was a wine vessel that became a unit of volume; @ evolved into shorthand for 'at' and appeared on typewriter keyboards in the 1880s; and the first use of @ in email dates to 1971.
- https://gulfnews.com/world/americas/ray-tomlinson-inventor-of-email-and--symbol-dies-1.1685430: Associated Press obituary of Ray Tomlinson (via Gulf News), read in full. Establishes: Tomlinson invented the first network person-to-person email in 1971 on ARPANET; it was not an assignment ('he was just fooling around'), the first messages went between two machines side by side and were 'entirely forgettable'; he chose the @ symbol to connect the username with the destination address; and in 2010 MoMA's Department of Architecture and Design added the @ symbol to its collection, crediting Tomlinson.
- https://www.britannica.com/topic/at-sign: Encyclopaedia Britannica, read (summary/lead). Corroborates that before the late 20th century the @ sign's primary use was commercial, signifying 'at the rate of,' and that it traces to the amphora/arroba unit of measure.

videos.title: Saturn is lighter than water.
videos.description:
Saturn is lighter than water. Not lighter in total. Lighter on average, per cubic centimetre, than the water in your kitchen tap. It is the only planet in the Solar System where that is true.

Saturn's mass compared with Earth's. Almost entirely hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements there are, stretched across a planet nine times Earth's width.

Only as a density comparison. There is no ocean anywhere near big enough, and if there were, the pressure at the bottom would stop the water from staying liquid. The density is real. The bathtub is not.

Ninety-five Earths' worth of mass, and still less dense than your bathwater.

videos.title: It cheats death. It does not skip ageing.
videos.description:
It cheats death. It does not skip ageing. Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from an adult jellyfish back into its earlier polyp stage when it is stressed, injured, or ageing. That part is real and published.

Described the reversal in the Biological Bulletin, using the phrase escaping death and achieving potential immortality, a title that outran the caveats inside its own paper.

Their colonies still get old. Aquarists who maintain polyp stock for years report it turning fragile after about six years: fewer healthy jellies, weaker responses. Reversing a life stage is not the same as not ageing.

Even the biologist who wrote it up says: I'm not convinced.

It is almost never wasabi. Most of what is served worldwide, and even much of what is served in Japan, is horseradish and mustard with green colouring standing in for the real plant.

A Stanford graduate student who won the five-player free-for-all, practising left-handed and two-fisted play against beginners just to keep his own games interesting.

A year of Rolling Stone magazine, and by one attendee's account, some beer Stewart Brand organised the tournament and covered it himself for a Rolling Stone feature, 'Fanatic Life and Symbolic Death Among the Computer Bums', published 7 December 1972.

The photographer covering it that night, Annie Leibovitz, would go on to take John Lennon's last professional photograph and portrait Queen Elizabeth II.

videos.title: It was nothing because thousands of programmers spent years making sure of it
videos.description:
It was nothing because thousands of programmers spent years making sure of it Two-digit year fields, standard practice in software written from the 1960s onward to save expensive memory, would have read '00' as 1900 once 1999 ticked over, breaking date maths across banking, aviation and power systems worldwide.

Appointed by President Clinton to chair the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion, reporting directly to the White House and coordinating the fix across every federal agency.

Precisely $8.05bn: what the US federal government alone spent finding and rewriting two-digit dates before the deadline. The Pentagon's own systems accounted for close to $3 billion of that.

They still run from about $100 billion to $600 billion No single audited figure exists for global spending: it depends on which industries and which countries get counted. Every serious estimate still lands in eleven figures.

Nothing breaking was the point. It was never proof there was nothing to fix.

videos.title: Nobody typed it on a phone.
videos.description:
Nobody typed it on a phone. It was sent from a computer. On 3 December 1992 an engineer at a desktop pushed two words onto the Vodafone network: Merry Christmas.

A 22-year-old test engineer, sending it to Vodafone director Richard Jarvis at the company Christmas party. His team had spent a year building the Short Message Service, meant not for chatting, but as a kind of pager.

He had no way to text back. Phones then could receive a message but not compose one. The reply came as a phone call, from the party, to say it had worked.

You could not text someone on a rival network until 1999. Handsets only gained a way to send texts in 1993, and every message was capped at 160 characters by the network's bandwidth: the pinch that bred txt spk like LOL.

The text that started it all got no text in reply: the phone could not send one.

Sources:
- https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/december-3/first-sms-text-message-sent: HISTORY (This Day in History), read in full. Establishes: on 3 December 1992 Neil Papworth, a 22-year-old engineer at Sema Group Telecoms, used a personal computer to send the first SMS, 'Merry Christmas', over the Vodafone network to Richard Jarvis, a Vodafone director, at a holiday party; Sema had hoped to use short messages as a paging service; Papworth got a phone call back saying it worked because cellphones could not yet send messages in reply; one year later Nokia released the first phone with an SMS feature; messages were limited to 160 characters due to bandwidth constraints; and cross-network texting was only possible from 1999.
- https://www.vodafone.com/news/newsroom/technology/25-anniversary-text-message: Vodafone (25th-anniversary article), read in full. Corroborates: Neil Papworth, 22, sent the first ever text from a computer to colleague Richard Jarvis on 3 December 1992, reading 'Merry Christmas,' while building an SMS for Vodafone; the 160-character limit; Nokia's 1993 SMS 'beep'; that texts could only be exchanged across networks from 1999; plus Papworth's own reflection that he had no idea texting would become so popular.

videos.title: Vikings beat him there by 471 years.
videos.description:
Vikings beat him there by 471 years. Not legend, a dated find: European wood, cut with metal tools nobody in the area had, at the northern tip of Newfoundland.

Nobody could say exactly when it was occupied for another 61 years. Archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad excavated it through the 1960s and dated it to "around 1000 AD" by comparing it with sites in Greenland and Iceland, a good estimate, not a year.

A cosmic-ray spike from the year 993 is baked into tree rings everywhere on Earth. Researchers counted growth rings outward from that marked ring, on wood the Norse had felled and shaped, straight to the year they cut it.

The exact year, from 127 radiocarbon measurements across four wooden objects. Not "around 1000". Not a century. One year.

Led the University of Groningen team that published the date in Nature, using the 993 solar storm as a fixed marker buried in the rings of every sample tested.

Sources:
- https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03972-8: Kuitems, M., Wallace, B.L., Lindsay, C. et al., "Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021," Nature (2021), read via abstract and multiple direct quotations in secondary science reporting (below). Establishes the AD 1021 date for Norse-cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows.
- https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/new-dating-method-shows-vikings-occupied-newfoundland-in-1021-ce-180978903/: Smithsonian Magazine, read directly. Establishes the method: a cosmic-ray-driven radiocarbon spike from a known solar storm in AD 993 is preserved in tree rings worldwide; researchers counted growth rings out from that marker ring to the bark edge on wood cut with metal blades, tools the region's Indigenous population did not have, landing on AD 1021.
- https://www.sciencenews.org/article/vikings-north-america-date-newfoundland: Science News, read directly. Establishes the numbers: 127 radiocarbon measurements across 83 tree rings from four wooden objects, three of which retained their outermost growth ring; calls it the oldest precise date for Europeans in the Americas and the only one predating Columbus's 1492 voyage.
- https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/nl/meadows/culture: Parks Canada, via search summary. Establishes site history: Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad found the site in 1960; archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad led excavations from 1961 to 1968 and identified it as Norse by comparison with Greenland and Iceland sites, dating it only broadly to around AD 1000; designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1968 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.

videos.title: It is now also a story about lawsuits actually being won.
videos.description:
It is now also a story about lawsuits actually being won. In 2021 her estate sued the companies that had profited for decades from her cells. Thermo Fisher Scientific settled in 2023. Novartis followed in 2026.

A 31 year old mother of five, treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital. Doctors took a tissue sample during her biopsy without telling her. She died the same year.

Hers doubled every 20 to 24 hours, and simply did not stop. Cell biologist George Gey's lab had collected samples from cancer patients for years. Lacks's were the first that would not die in a dish, the first human cell line to survive indefinitely outside a body.

The count of scientific papers built on HeLa cells by 2009 alone, and still climbing then by more than 300 a month.

In the 1980s, a scientist found the virus that had caused her cancer, still living in her cells. Harald zur Hausen identified HPV18 in the original HeLa sample, the same virus that had caused Lacks's cervical cancer. The discovery won him a Nobel Prize and led directly to the HPV vaccine.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa: read in full. Established that cells were taken from Henrietta Lacks on 8 February 1951 without her knowledge during treatment for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital, that she died on 4 October 1951 aged 31, that cell biologist George Otto Gey found the cells doubled every 20 to 24 hours where every previous sample had died within days, that by 2009 more than 60,000 scientific papers had used HeLa cells and the count was rising by over 300 a month, that Harald zur Hausen found HPV18 in the original sample in the 1980s and later won a Nobel Prize for linking HPV to cervical cancer, and the 2021 lawsuit against Thermo Fisher Scientific, its August 2023 settlement, and the 2026 Novartis settlement.
- https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/henriettalacks: Johns Hopkins Medicine, read in full. Established the institution's own account: gynaecologist Dr Howard Jones found the tumour, a sample went to Gey's lab, Lacks died on 4 October 1951, and Johns Hopkins's own statement that it has never sold or profited from the HeLa cell line but 'could have, and should have, done more' to inform and work with the Lacks family.

This building sends some of it back up. In the mid-1930s, General Electric wired cameras and recording equipment to the Empire State Building to study its lightning. They found tall enough buildings can throw bolts upward, from the ground into the cloud.

videos.title: That is not a figure of speech.
videos.description:
That is not a figure of speech. The lining of your gut holds a real, dense network of neurons, running from your oesophagus to your rectum, with its own name: the enteric nervous system.

Columbia gastroenterologist who coined the term second brain and wrote the book on it, arguing the gut's nervous system deserved to be studied as more than plumbing.

It can run with the brain disconnected. It has more neurons than your spinal cord, uses over thirty of the same signalling chemicals as your brain, and keeps working in a gut removed entirely from the body.

It cannot think for you. It can absolutely talk to you.

videos.title: It runs a formula and reads you the next line of a script.
videos.description:
It runs a formula and reads you the next line of a script. Same starting seed, same sequence, every time. Nothing is chosen; it is all pre-computed. That is why they are called pseudo-random.

He built the first computer method for it (square a number, keep the middle digits, repeat) for Monte Carlo runs on ENIAC. He also warned exactly what it was.

Anyone who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin. His point: no formula is truly random. He used them anyway (hundreds of times faster than reading random numbers off punch cards), knowing precisely what they were.

Hit the wrong number and it spits zeros forever. The middle-square method can collapse to zero, or fall into a short loop, and never recover. Von Neumann counted that a virtue: a failure you can at least catch.

Even an AI's flashes of randomness are a formula quietly choosing the next number.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-square_method: read in full. Establishes: the middle-square method (square an n-digit number, take the middle n digits, repeat) was invented by John von Neumann and described at a 1949 conference (papers reprinted 1951 as 'Various techniques used in connection with random digits,' Monte Carlo Method, NBS Applied Mathematics Series vol. 12); von Neumann's quip 'Anyone who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin,' meaning no strict arithmetic procedure is truly random; that he used them anyway because they were hundreds of times faster than reading random numbers off punch cards, important for his ENIAC work; and that the method degenerates: if the middle digits become all zeroes it outputs zeroes forever, and it can fall into short cycles.
- https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys466/sp2013/lnotes/random_numbers.html: University of Illinois PHYS 466 course notes (Ceperley/Johnson), read in full. Corroborates the von Neumann 1951 quote; distinguishes truly random (e.g. Geiger counts of radioactive decay) from pseudo-random (deterministic, with a repeating period) and quasi-random; states plainly that 'computers as they are now constructed are deterministic' and that everyone uses PRNGs, a mapping s(n+1)=f(s(n)) seeded from something like the clock; and notes true hardware randomness is avoided as too slow and expensive.

That one hidden battery helped kill Nintendo's own disk drive.

videos.title: It is still online, at its original address.
videos.description:
It is still online, at its original address. info.cern.ch: a page about a project called WorldWideWeb, written by Tim Berners-Lee. It had to explain what hypertext was, because almost nobody had seen a link.

Berners-Lee wrote the first browser and ran the first server on a single black computer built by Steve Jobs's other company. In the beginning the entire web lived on that one machine, in one office.

Switch off that one cube and the web went dark. So it wore a warning in red ink: This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN. The cube sits in a CERN museum now, label and all.

The web was a side project at a particle collider. CERN builds machines to smash atoms; the web was built so its scientists could share papers. HTML, HTTP and the URL all came out of it, and in 1993 CERN gave them away, free, into the public domain.

The first web page had exactly one job: to explain what a web page was.

Sources:
- https://home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/short-history-web/: CERN's official short history of the Web, read in full. Establishes: Berners-Lee had the first web server and browser running at CERN by the end of 1990 on a NeXT computer kept in his office; the machine carried a hand-written label in red ink reading 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'; info.cern.ch was the address of the world's first website and server; the first web page was http://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html, describing the WWW project, hypertext and how to run a server; the software was announced on Internet newsgroups in August 1991; and on 30 April 1993 CERN placed the WorldWideWeb source code in the public domain, royalty-free.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WorldWideWeb: read in full. Confirms Berners-Lee wrote the WorldWideWeb browser/editor on a NeXT Computer during the second half of 1990, completed 'some time before' 25 December 1990 after about two months' work, released to the public in August 1991; that it was both the first web browser and the first WYSIWYG HTML editor; and that CERN released the source into the public domain on 30 April 1993.
- https://boingboing.net/2008/07/09/firstever-web-server.html: Cory Doctorow (Boing Boing), read in full, quoting the Wikipedia image caption for the NeXTcube: it was Berners-Lee's first Web server, is kept in the Microcosm museum at CERN's Meyrin site, the document on its keyboard is his 'Information Management: A Proposal', and the label reads 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!', used to corroborate the sticker wording and the machine's preservation.

videos.title: The men who measured him used a different ruler than you're picturing.
videos.description:
The men who measured him used a different ruler than you're picturing. His valet, a general and his own physician all recorded the same figure: five pieds, two pouces. That is French feet and inches, not English ones.

He comes out at roughly five foot six. A French pouce measured 2.7 centimetres against the English inch's 2.54. Do the sum and Napoleon lands just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of his time.

British cartoonist who invented 'Little Boney', a diminutive, raving caricature of Napoleon, in response to a real outburst the emperor made at the British ambassador on 14 March 1803. Gillray kept shrinking him for years afterwards.

By 1804 he was drawn six inches tall. Gillray's cartoons showed Napoleon as an animal, then a baby, then a Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver'. The caricature, not the ruler, is what stuck.

Napoleon himself said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.

Sources:
- https://www.history.com/articles/napoleon-complex-short - HISTORY (Una McIlvenna, 13 November 2019, updated 10 July 2025), read in full. Established that three French sources, Napoleon's valet Constant, General Gourgaud and his physician Francesco Antommarchi, recorded his height as '5 pieds 2 pouces'; that the French pouce measured 2.7cm against the imperial inch's 2.54cm, so the true figure converts to roughly 1.67 metres, just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of the early 1800s; that the 'short Napoleon' image is largely the work of British cartoonist James Gillray (1756-1815); that Gillray's earliest Napoleon cartoons (1798) showed him boastful but not small; that the diminutive 'Little Boney' image began with Gillray's 1803 cartoon 'Maniac-Ravings, or Little Boney in a Strong Fit', satirising a real outburst by Napoleon against the British ambassador, Lord Whitworth, at the Tuileries on 14 March 1803; that Gillray's 1805 cartoon 'The Plumb-pudding in Danger', described as probably the most famous political cartoon of all time, shows Napoleon at half the size of British Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger; and that Napoleon reportedly said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.
- https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/little-boney/ - The Public Domain Review (Peter W. Walker, Assistant Professor of History, University of Wyoming, 21 March 2024), read in full. Established that Gillray produced around forty of the more than two thousand British satirical prints of Napoleon and that his were the most influential; that Gillray's 1798 cartoon still drew Napoleon as 'average-sized'; that the caricature shrank progressively through 1803 as invasion fears grew, becoming an animal in 'Death of the Corsican Fox', a baby in 'The Genius of France', and a six-inch Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver' (1804); that other cartoonists copied the trope; and that the term 'Napoleon Complex' derives directly from this caricature legacy and is described as being of questionable scientific validity.

videos.description:
He said women were hung on meat hooks and drained into wine bottles. Neither was in it. On 9 December 1993, Senator Joseph Lieberman, joined by Herbert Kohl and Byron Dorgan, held hearings condemning the Sega CD game Night Trap using details that were not actually part of its plot.

Senator for Connecticut. Opened a press conference on 1 December 1993 denouncing 'violent video games', flanked by the National PTA and former Captain Kangaroo star Bob Keeshan, then led the December hearings naming Mortal Kombat and Night Trap directly.

Nintendo and Sega mostly used the hearing to blame each other Nintendo's Howard Lincoln, a former trial lawyer, and Sega's Bill White turned their testimony into their console war, each pointing at the other's catalogue rather than defending the industry.

Congress never passed Lieberman's ratings bill. The industry built its own system first, and still runs it today.

videos.title: It is still online, at its original address.
videos.description:
It is still online, at its original address. info.cern.ch: a page about a project called WorldWideWeb, written by Tim Berners-Lee. It had to explain what hypertext was, because almost nobody had seen a link.

Berners-Lee wrote the first browser and ran the first server on a single black computer built by Steve Jobs's other company. In the beginning the entire web lived on that one machine, in one office.

Switch off that one cube and the web went dark. So it wore a warning in red ink: This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN. The cube sits in a CERN museum now, label and all.

The web was a side project at a particle collider. CERN builds machines to smash atoms; the web was built so its scientists could share papers. HTML, HTTP and the URL all came out of it, and in 1993 CERN gave them away, free, into the public domain.

The first web page had exactly one job: to explain what a web page was.

Sources:
- https://home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/short-history-web/: CERN's official short history of the Web, read in full. Establishes: Berners-Lee had the first web server and browser running at CERN by the end of 1990 on a NeXT computer kept in his office; the machine carried a hand-written label in red ink reading 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'; info.cern.ch was the address of the world's first website and server; the first web page was http://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html, describing the WWW project, hypertext and how to run a server; the software was announced on Internet newsgroups in August 1991; and on 30 April 1993 CERN placed the WorldWideWeb source code in the public domain, royalty-free.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WorldWideWeb: read in full. Confirms Berners-Lee wrote the WorldWideWeb browser/editor on a NeXT Computer during the second half of 1990, completed 'some time before' 25 December 1990 after about two months' work, released to the public in August 1991; that it was both the first web browser and the first WYSIWYG HTML editor; and that CERN released the source into the public domain on 30 April 1993.
- https://boingboing.net/2008/07/09/firstever-web-server.html: Cory Doctorow (Boing Boing), read in full, quoting the Wikipedia image caption for the NeXTcube: it was Berners-Lee's first Web server, is kept in the Microcosm museum at CERN's Meyrin site, the document on its keyboard is his 'Information Management: A Proposal', and the label reads 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!', used to corroborate the sticker wording and the machine's preservation.

videos.title: Most days, three to eight people actually showed up.
videos.description:
Most days, three to eight people actually showed up. The 1955 proposal asked the Rockefeller Foundation to fund '10 men' for '2 months'. Only three of them, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and Ray Solomonoff, stayed for the entire eight weeks.

Wrote the funding proposal with Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, and coined the field's name inside it. He wanted a neutral term, anything but 'cybernetics', which would have meant working under the combative Norbert Wiener.

Newell and Simon showed a program that already reasoned. Their Logic Theory Machine used symbolic logic to prove mathematical theorems. In 1975 they won computing's highest honour, the Turing Award, for the work it began.

How long the workshop actually ran, from 18 June to 17 August 1956, by the attendees' own notes. It is usually remembered as six.

The dictionary they used to look up 'heuristic' is still in that room.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop: read in full. Established the 1955 proposal text quoted directly (a '2 month, 10 man study'), that John McCarthy coined the term 'artificial intelligence' in that document and chose it partly to avoid 'cybernetics' and Norbert Wiener, that the workshop ran roughly eight weeks (about 18 June to 17 August 1956) by Ray Solomonoff's own contemporaneous notes though it is usually said to be six weeks, that only McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and Solomonoff stayed the full time, and that daily attendance ranged from about three to eight people.
- https://spectrum.ieee.org/dartmouth-ai-workshop: Grace Solomonoff, IEEE Spectrum, read in full. Confirmed the exact dates (18 June to 17 August 1956), established that Herbert Simon and Allen Newell presented the Logic Theory Machine that summer and later won the 1975 Turing Award for the ideas behind it, and that in 2006 Trenchard More located the same dictionary the group had used to look up 'heuristic', still in the room where the workshop was held.

videos.title: He accused IBM of secretly using a human grandmaster.
videos.description:
He accused IBM of secretly using a human grandmaster. After Deep Blue beat the reigning world chess champion in 1997, Garry Kasparov refused to believe a machine had done it. It echoed 18th and 19th century chess-automaton hoaxes, in which a hidden person, not the machine, did the actual playing.

Moves 36 and 37 in one game looked too human to be brute force. Kasparov and grandmaster observers felt the moves were too sophisticated for a machine playing by raw calculation. IBM denied any human intervention beyond fixing bugs between games.

A glitch made Deep Blue pick a move at random rather than its best-calculated one. One of the machine's own designers has said a fail-safe kicked in when the computer couldn't settle on a move, and Kasparov read the random result as a sign of deeper strategy than was actually there.

Custom chess-only processors built into the machine, working in parallel. Not learning, not intuition, just purpose-built calculation at scale.

IBM never gave him one. Deep Blue's exact fate after 1997 is described differently by different accounts, but every account agrees on this: the third match Kasparov wanted never happened.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_versus_Garry_Kasparov - read in full 1 Sep 2026: Kasparov won the 1996 Philadelphia match 4-2; Deep Blue won the 1997 New York rematch 3.5-2.5, the first defeat of a reigning world chess champion by a computer under standard tournament conditions; Game 1's move 44 was allegedly the result of a bug, in which Deep Blue, unable to settle on a move, resorted to a fail-safe; after losing Game 2 in a position later shown to be drawable, Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, alleging a grandmaster had made moves for the machine, specifically 36.axb5 and 37.Be4; the article's own lead states that although it was reported IBM had dismantled Deep Blue afterward, it in fact remained in operation for several years.
- https://theconversation.com/twenty-years-on-from-deep-blue-vs-kasparov-how-a-chess-match-started-the-big-data-revolution-76882 - read in full 1 Sep 2026: academic retrospective corroborating the cheating accusation and IBM's denial (stating the only human intervention was fixing bugs between games); adds that Kasparov's suspicion echoed 18th and 19th century chess-automaton hoaxes; grandmaster John Nunn called one Deep Blue move 'stunning' and 'exceptional'; one of Deep Blue's own designers has said a glitch made the machine pick a move at random rather than its calculated best, which Kasparov read as deeper strategy; the final configuration of the machine controlled 480 custom integrated circuits designed specifically to play chess; IBM refused Kasparov's request for a rematch.

videos.title: 1920, in a Czech play.
videos.description:
1920, in a Czech play. It appears for the first time in Karel Capek's R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots), published in 1920 and staged in Prague in 1921. Before that, the word did not exist.

It means forced labour. From the Czech 'robota': the unpaid drudgery a serf owed his lord. The deeper Slavic root, 'rab', means slave. The name was built to mean bondage.

They were artificial people. Rossum's robots are not clanking machines but mass-produced living workers, grown rather than built, far closer to lab-made humans than to anything with gears.

The robots rise and end humanity. The very first tale to use the word is also the first robot uprising. By the final act, mankind is gone. The trope arrived fully formed, a century ago.

Our word for machines was coined for slaves made of flesh.

Sources:
- https://www.britannica.com/topic/RUR: Encyclopaedia Britannica, read directly: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots), a three-act play by Karel Capek, published 1920 and performed 1921; 'Capek invented the word robot (derived from the Czech word for forced labour)'; a scientist Rossum creates humanlike beings who are mass-produced and eventually come to dominate humanity.
- https://thereader.mitpress.mit.edu/origin-word-robot-rur/: MIT Press Reader (John M. Jordan, adapted from his book 'Robots'), read directly: R.U.R. premiered in Prague in 1921; the word derives from Czech 'robota' (forced labour as done by serfs), Slavic root 'rab' meaning slave; the original robots 'more accurately define androids... neither metallic nor mechanical'; in the play the robots revolt and mankind 'is no more'; the play was translated into 30+ languages soon after.

videos.title: Pull a list down, let go, it refreshes.
videos.description:
Pull a list down, let go, it refreshes. Nobody built it into the phone. One developer invented it for a Twitter app, and it spread into everything: Mail, Chrome, Instagram, Facebook.

Ex-Apple, one of five people on the first iPhone. He wrote the Twitter app Tweetie alone. Version 1.0 hid a refresh button in a corner, and he wanted the corner back, so he turned refreshing into a pull.

He built it in a single afternoon. Two iterations, no user testing, shipped in Tweetie 2.0 in 2009. He tuned the pull distance by hand until it felt right, then moved on.

By 2013 it held a patent on the pull. Brichter was uneasy about that, so he made Twitter agree, as a condition of the sale, that it would never use the patent to attack anyone. It is allowed to defend, and nothing more.

The same downward pull is now studied as a slot-machine lever, for the refresh you cannot stop reaching for.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pull-to-refresh (read in full 26 Aug 2026): the pull-to-refresh gesture was developed by Loren Brichter and first appeared in Tweetie, an iOS Twitter app he built as a personal project in 2008 after leaving Apple in 2007; Tweetie 1.0 placed a refresh button at the top of the list, which he wanted to replace to reclaim the screen space; the two iterations of the gesture were, in Wikipedia's words, 'created in a single afternoon with no user testing'; it shipped in Tweetie 2.0; it was later added to Chrome (optional 2015, mandatory since 2019) and Firefox (2020 to 2021); and it has been criticised for resembling a lever on a gambling machine and so feeding social-media addiction.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loren_Brichter (read in full 26 Aug 2026): Brichter, born 1984, worked at Apple from 2006 to 2007 on a five-person team making the first iPhone's graphics hardware and software communicate; founded atebits in 2007; released Tweetie in 2008; won an Apple Design Award in 2009; and atebits with Tweetie were bought by Twitter in 2010, after which Tweetie became the official Twitter for iPhone.

videos.title: Work 25 minutes. Break. Repeat.
videos.description:
Work 25 minutes. Break. Repeat. The man who invented it calls that a distortion. 'The iconic 25-minute sessions,' Francesco Cirillo writes, 'aren't the technique. They're just one expression of it.'

A university student who could not concentrate, timing himself with the first thing to hand on the kitchen counter: a wind-up timer shaped like a tomato. Pomodoro is simply Italian for tomato.

Not 25 minutes. Two. 'Can I study for just two minutes without interruption?' The famous 25 came later, and even that, he says, is one expression of the method, not the point of it.

His answer: even none is fine. 'Your goal isn't to complete Pomodoros,' he says, 'it's to become aware of what happens in your mind.' A focus method whose own author does not care how much you get done.

Sources:
- https://www.pomodorotechnique.com/francesco-cirillo/ (Francesco Cirillo's official site; read in full 26 Aug 2026): in his own words, 'I created the Pomodoro Technique in the 1980s with a tomato-shaped kitchen timer and a problem: I couldn't focus on my university studies', and the first experiment was 'Can I study for just two minutes without interruption?'. Under 'Distortion' he writes that newspapers, bloggers and apps 'reduced the entire technique to a single instruction: Work for 25 minutes, then take a break', and that 'The iconic 25-minute timer sessions aren't the technique, they're just one expression of this broader mindset'. On goals he writes, 'Even one Pomodoro, or none, is fine. Your goal isn't to complete Pomodoros. Your goal is to become aware of what happens in your mind'. Pomodoro is Italian for tomato.

videos.title: runs on an algorithm built for a robot.
videos.description:
runs on an algorithm built for a robot. A* is the standard for pathfinding in games and maps. It was written in 1968 to help one machine cross a cluttered room without walking into things.

At Stanford Research Institute, plotting routes for Shakey, a robot so unsteady that the team named it for the way it rattled and shook whenever it moved.

The star arrived with a proof. Raphael refined it; Hart showed that, given an honest guess of the distance left, it always finds the shortest path. A* meant: we can prove this one is optimal.

It isn't. Even a co-author first guessed it came from Kleene-star syntax. Hart says no: it's the statistician's star for an optimal value. The real meaning went unrecorded for fifty years.

Gaming's smartest navigator is named after a robot that couldn't hold still.

Sources:
- https://cacm.acm.org/opinion/a-search/: Communications of the ACM viewpoint, read directly: A* was published in 1968 by Hart, Nilsson and Raphael; the authors themselves recount that Nilsson devised it to plan Shakey the Robot's route through a room of obstacles and first called it 'Algorithm A'; Raphael improved it and Hart proved it optimal given an admissible heuristic, so they named it A* 'to distinguish it from any simpler algorithm A'; Hart says the star denotes an optimal value (from statistics) and 'has nothing whatsoever to do with Kleene star syntax', while co-author Nilsson initially guessed the Kleene interpretation; the meaning had gone undocumented until this piece.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakey_the_robot: Wikipedia, read directly: Shakey was developed ~1966-1972 at the AI Center of Stanford Research Institute (SRI); A* was one of its notable results; the name came from its tall build and 'tendency to shake', quoted: 'it shakes like hell and moves around, let's just call it Shakey.'

videos.title: The aliens were the third choice, not the first.
videos.description:
The aliens were the third choice, not the first. Tomohiro Nishikado wanted tanks first. He wanted them to face forward to look right, and that stopped working the moment the enemies had to move sideways.

Designer at Taito. After tanks, he tried planes, but the hardware of the time could not animate believable flight. Aliens worked because jerky, mechanical movement did not look like a mistake on them.

He says it was not about Star Wars. Space Invaders shipped a year after Star Wars and people have assumed a connection ever since. Nishikado's own account credits animation limits and a tank that looked wrong, not the movie.

A cornering problem invented the alien shooter.

videos.title: A computer was a person.
videos.description:
A computer was a person. Someone whose whole job was arithmetic, done by hand. When the machines came, they took the name from the people who did the work, not the other way round.

First to put the word "computer" into English, in a book of advice. He praised a man as "the truest computer ... the best arithmetician that ever breathed." A line about a person, not a machine.

NASA still hired human computers in the 1960s. Katherine Johnson joined NACA's West Area Computing pool, Black women doing the maths by hand, in 1953. She worked out the flight paths for Alan Shepard in 1961 and John Glenn in 1962.

The machine did not coin the word. It inherited it from the people doing the sums.

Sources:
- https://www.computinghistory.org.uk/det/5829/Richard-Braithwaite-coined-the-phrase-computer/ - The Centre for Computing History, read in full. Established that the first recorded English use of the word "computer" is in Richard Braithwaite's 1613 book The Yong Mans Gleanings, describing a person as "the truest computer ... the best arithmetician that ever breathed", that "computer" meant a person who calculated by hand until the 1950s, and that NASA employed human computers such as Katherine Johnson.
- https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/nasas-west-area-computers/ - Via search summary. Established that NASA's West Area Computers at Langley were Black women who did the calculations by hand, that Katherine Johnson joined NACA's West Area Computing pool in 1953, and that she did the trajectory work for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight and John Glenn's 1962 orbit.

videos.title: It was built to say hello.
videos.description:
It was built to say hello. In 1971, a program called Creeper moved between machines on ARPANET, the internet's ancestor, and printed a message rather than deleting or stealing anything.

At BBN, wrote Creeper for the PDP-10 operating system TENEX. It displayed: I'M THE CREEPER, CATCH ME IF YOU CAN.

The absolute most computers Creeper could ever infect, because that was the entire population of TENEX machines then on ARPANET.

It got hunted down on purpose. Ray Tomlinson, who separately built the first networked email, wrote a program called Reaper in 1972 whose only job was to find Creeper and delete it. The first virus. The first antivirus.

The internet's first infection topped out at 28 machines.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creeper_and_Reaper

videos.title: Everest only wins on one ruler.
videos.description:
Everest only wins on one ruler. It is the highest point above sea level, 8,848 metres. But height above the sea is one measurement of several, and it is the only one Everest tops.

Mauna Kea in Hawaii, measured from its base on the Pacific floor to its summit. That makes the Hawaiian volcano the tallest mountain on Earth, over a kilometre taller than Everest. Only about 4,205 metres of it stand above the water.

A third mountain wins, and it is the shortest. Earth bulges at the equator, so Ecuador's Chimborazo, sitting almost on it, pushes its peak 2,072 metres farther from the planet's core than Everest's while standing lower above the sea. NOAA calls it the closest point on Earth to the stars.

Highest, tallest, farthest out. Three mountains, three different rulers.

Sources:
- https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/highestpoint.html (NOAA National Ocean Service, National Geodetic Survey; read in full 26 Aug 2026): establishes that Mount Everest is the highest point above global mean sea level at 8,848 metres; that Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the tallest mountain from base to peak, rising more than 10,210 metres from the Pacific floor to its summit with only about 4,205 metres of it above the water; and that because Earth bulges at the equator from its rotation, the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo, one degree south of the equator, sits over 2,072 metres farther from Earth's centre than Everest's summit even though Chimborazo is only 6,268 metres above sea level, which NOAA calls the closest point on Earth to the stars.

videos.title: The designer built it to refuse to be that.
videos.description:
The designer built it to refuse to be that. Atari's coin-op boss saw a radar-screen photo in a magazine and told his team to make a game like it. The junior programmer he handed it to had other ideas.

A junior programmer, fresh off his first game, Atari Soccer. Given a one-line brief about Soviet missiles and an American defence, he attached two conditions of his own before writing a line of code.

Condition two: you could never fire back. Theurer refused to give the player a retaliation button. In his own words: 'I did not want to put the player in a position of being a genocidal maniac.' Mutual destruction wasn't a game mechanic to him.

Eureka, San Francisco, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, San Diego. The whole California coast, named outright in early versions. Theurer stripped the names before release, leaving the geography to the player's imagination.

Theurer dreamed about the nuclear blast he was coding. They didn't stop when the game shipped in June 1980, they just came less often. The ending reflects it: the screen doesn't say 'Game Over.' It says 'THE END.' There is no way to win.

videos.title: The Great Wall of China is visible from space.
videos.description:
The Great Wall of China is visible from space. It's repeated so often it feels like common knowledge. It has never been true, and how the claim got started is stranger than the myth itself.

It comes from a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not cartoon. Nobody had been to space yet. The claim wasn't a report of what someone saw, it was a guess, printed as fact, decades before Yuri Gagarin's first orbital flight in 1961.

China's first astronaut. After 14 orbits aboard Shenzhou 5, he came back down and told reporters the scenery was beautiful, but he hadn't seen the Great Wall. China's own education ministry then corrected a textbook that had taught the myth as fact.

Apollo's Neil Armstrong said no human structures are visible from the Moon. Shuttle astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman put it plainly: he never saw the Great Wall. From low orbit, under near-perfect light, the wall is sometimes barely visible, and easily mistaken for an ordinary road.

videos.title: A horse could allegedly do arithmetic.
videos.description:
A horse could allegedly do arithmetic. Hans tapped out answers to maths, calendar and spelling questions with his hoof. A formal commission of thirteen experts examined him in 1904 and found no trick at all.

In 1907, Oskar Pfungst found the trick anyway. Hans wasn't calculating. He was reading his questioner's posture and expression, and stopping the instant they subtly relaxed.

Correct, when Hans could see a questioner who already knew the answer. Hide that questioner from view and he collapsed to 6 percent.

The psychologist assigned to re-test Hans. He proved his theory by becoming the horse himself: tapping out numbers by hand, he produced the same involuntary tell in the people standing beside him.

The pattern outlived the horse. "Clever Hans effect" is now the term for an AI model that looks intelligent while actually keying off a spurious signal, an image classifier reading text in a photo instead of the picture itself.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans: read in full. Establishes: Hans, a horse owned by Wilhelm von Osten in Berlin, appeared to add, subtract, multiply, divide, tell time and spell by tapping his hoof; a thirteen-person commission convened by philosopher Carl Stumpf concluded in September 1904 that no tricks were involved; psychologist Oskar Pfungst re-investigated and in 1907 found Hans answered correctly 89% of the time (50 of 56) when he could see a questioner who knew the answer, but only 6% (2 of 35) when he could not see the questioner; Pfungst traced this to involuntary postural and facial cues the questioner gave off approaching the correct tap count; "Clever Hans effect" is now used in machine learning for a model whose apparent competence comes from a spurious signal rather than the intended task, for example an image classifier that reads text in a photo instead of analysing the image.

at Danisco, found that the surviving bacteria had copied new DNA sequences from the attacking viruses into a repeating region of their genome called CRISPR, making them immune to that exact virus next time.

videos.description:
Venus takes 243 Earth days to complete a single rotation, but only 224.7 Earth days to complete one full orbit of the Sun. Both figures are measured against the fixed stars: the sidereal rotation period and the sidereal year.

how long a single spin of Venus takes, measured against the stars. Its year takes only 224.7.

Venus also spins backwards. Almost every planet rotates the same direction it orbits the Sun; Venus turns the opposite way, a quirk called retrograde rotation. Venus is the only planet in the Solar System whose day, measured this way, is longer than its year.

Combine the backwards spin with the orbit and the result is stranger still: measured sunrise to sunrise, a Venusian day lasts about 117 Earth days, roughly half a Venusian year. This sunrise-to-sunrise figure, the solar day, is a different measurement from the 243-day sidereal day above, and the two should not be mixed up.

If you could stand on the surface and see through Venus's clouds, which you cannot, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east, the reverse of Earth.

videos.description:
None of them are actually seeds, and the fruit isn't a berry. Botanically, a strawberry fails the definition of a berry on every count that matters.

A strawberry's flower has dozens of separate ones. That single-ovary rule is why bananas, grapes, tomatoes and even cucumbers count as true berries, while strawberries, raspberries and blackberries don't.

It's the swollen base of the flower. What botanists call the receptacle grows large and fleshy around the true fruits, rather than the flesh coming from any ovary wall, which is how a true berry is built.

are the actual fruits, not seeds. Each dot is a separate dry fruit called an achene, and each one holds a single true seed sealed inside it.

The avocado, with its single huge seed, meets the botanical definition of a berry. The strawberry, with hundreds of visible seeds, doesn't.

Sources:
- https://www.britannica.com/science/berry-plant-reproductive-body - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Encyclopaedia Britannica, last updated 1 September 2026. - https://sciencenotes.org/is-a-strawberry-a-berry-why-the-answer-is-surprisingly-no/ - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Science Notes (Anne Helmenstine, published 27 June 2026).
