videos.title: When threatened, a bombardier beetle mixes two chemicals stored in separate sacs inside its abdomen
videos.description:
When threatened, a bombardier beetle mixes two chemicals stored in separate sacs inside its abdomen and fires the reaction straight at whatever is attacking it, with an audible pop. Natural History Museum beetle curator Max Barclay explains that a handful of related beetles use milder chemical defences, but bombardier beetles took the idea to an extreme.

The chemicals are hydrogen peroxide and a hydroquinone, and mixing them is a genuinely violent reaction: the spray comes out scalding hot and under real pressure, fired in rapid pulses rather than one continuous stream. A tough chamber at the rear of the abdomen contains the reaction, so even an accidental discharge just fires harmlessly out the back rather than injuring the beetle itself.

roughly how hot the beetle's defensive spray gets, hot enough that one species, the African bombardier beetle, can aim it in almost any direction, including back over its own body.

In an 1846 letter, Darwin described grabbing two ground beetles by hand and, rather than let a third species escape, popping one of the beetles into his mouth. It responded by firing its chemical defence down his throat. The beetle in that story was a close relative of true bombardier beetles rather than one itself, but a demonstration of the same basic strategy.

The defence still works after a beetle has already been eaten. In one study, Japanese toads that swallowed bombardier beetles vomited 43% of them back up alive, mostly within 12 to 107 minutes, and more than 93% of those survivors were still alive at least two weeks later.

videos.description:
On 10 July 1913, a station at Greenland Ranch in Death Valley reportedly reached 134 degrees Fahrenheit, and the World Meteorological Organization formally certified it as the world record in 2012, after a rival 1922 reading from Libya was found to be invalid. It remains the officially certified figure today, recorded during a ten day stretch that also produced several days above 129 degrees.

That 2025 study, led by University of Alabama meteorologist Roy Spencer, compared the 1913 reading against a century of July data from nearby stations at similar elevation. The team estimated the real temperature at Greenland Ranch that day was closer to 120 degrees Fahrenheit, some 14 degrees below the certified figure.

Their leading explanation is not equipment failure but a person: ranch foreman Oscar Denton, who photographic evidence suggests moved the station's thermometer shelter to a hotter, bare ground site without official approval. The study also raises the possibility that he substituted readings from unofficial veranda thermometers, some of which locals reported as showing 135 degrees or hotter that same week.

No formal World Meteorological Organization review has been opened, so the 134 degree figure keeps its certification for now. One independent climatologist called the newer study convincing precisely because it draws on many surrounding stations rather than a single comparison point.

Each of an octopus's eight arms contains its own cluster of neurons, letting it taste, touch and move on its own without waiting for an instruction from the centre. The Natural History Museum's Jon Ablett, who cares for the museum's cephalopod collection, says this lets the arms complete tasks faster and more effectively than a single central controller could manage alone.

roughly how many neurons a common octopus has, about as many as a dog, with two thirds of them distributed through its arms rather than its head.

The arms are not entirely independent, though. A 2011 experiment sent an octopus's arm through a maze it could not feel its way through, forcing it to rely on eyesight instead. Most of the octopuses tested successfully guided the arm to food using only visual information processed by the central, doughnut shaped brain wrapped around the animal's oesophagus, proving the centre can still take top down control when needed.

Haemocyanin carries oxygen more efficiently in cold, low oxygen water, which suits ocean life well. Deoxygenated, the blood loses its colour and turns clear.

Three separate hearts keep that blue blood moving: one circulates it around the body, and two exist purely to push it past the gills to pick up oxygen.

In 1934, British engineer Robert Rule Graham identified three separate wing structures that let them do it. He called them the comb, the fringe and the velvet, each solving a different part of the noise problem.

A row of stiff, comb-like serrations along the leading edge of the wing breaks up incoming air into smaller, quieter streams before it can build into noisy turbulence. This is the structure most modern engineering copies have focused on.

A soft, ragged fringe along the back edge of the wing smooths the air as it leaves, while a velvety layer of down across the wing itself soaks up whatever high-frequency sound is left. Together the three structures strip out almost all the whooshing sound other birds' wings make.

a British aeronautical engineer and ornithologist, was the first to describe all three of these structures and connect them to the owl's silence.

It was built to catch the network's mistakes. In 2015, engineers needed a way to check whether a trained neural network had learned the right thing, not just the popular thing.

Wombat faeces come out as near perfect cubes, flat sides and corners included, even though the gut they travel through is round from one end to the other. Georgia Tech mechanical engineer David Hu and University of Tasmania wildlife ecologist Scott Carver set out to work out how, and the pair won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize for the answer.

Carver, who dissects wombats that have been humanely put down for his conservation research, was the one who first noticed where the shape actually forms. Richard Feynman never named that method, and there is no evidence he used it as a formal system. The four step version taught online today (pick a concept, explain it simply, spot where you get stuck, return to the source) was written up by somebody else, decades after he died.

Preparing for his Princeton oral exams, he opened a notebook and wrote on the title page: NOTEBOOK OF THINGS I DON'T KNOW ABOUT. Biographer James Gleick describes him spending weeks taking every branch of physics apart, hunting for the gaps and inconsistencies himself, not teaching it to an imaginary student.

The notebook was real. The technique named after it was invented by somebody else, long after.

videos.title: Ordinary sinks, baths and toilets do not drain in different directions depending on hemisphere.
videos.description:
Ordinary sinks, baths and toilets do not drain in different directions depending on hemisphere. The force involved is real, but at the size of a household drain it is far too small to matter. What actually decides the direction is the shape of the basin and whatever swirl the water already had before the plug came out.

In 1962, MIT's Ascher Shapiro built a still, circular tank two metres across, covered it, and left the water to settle for at least 24 hours before pulling the plug. Ordinary tap water is never that still. Filling a sink, or even a previous flush, leaves swirl in the water that completely overwhelms the effect he was trying to isolate.

How long Shapiro left his two metre tank undisturbed before draining it, just to remove the residual motion that ruins the effect in an ordinary sink or bath.

The tank took 20 minutes to fully drain, and a small wooden cross floating above the plug hole did not begin turning until roughly 15 minutes in. By the end it was rotating once every three to four seconds, consistently anticlockwise, matching the direction the effect predicts for the Northern Hemisphere.

Mechanical engineer at MIT. His basin experiment was later checked in the Southern Hemisphere by mathematician Lloyd Trefethen, who ran five tests at the University of Sydney, each left to settle for 18 hours or more, and recorded rotation in the opposite direction every time.

Two research teams, a decade and a hemisphere apart, needed a covered tank and a full day of stillness to see an effect your toilet will never show you.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force - Read in full. States plainly that bathtubs, toilets and other water receptacles do not drain in opposite directions by hemisphere because the Coriolis force is negligible at that scale, and that drain direction instead comes down to the geometry of the drain and receptacle plus whatever motion the water already had; describes Ascher Shapiro's 1962 MIT experiment using a covered 2 metre tank left to settle for at least 24 hours, a small wooden cross to display rotation, a 20 minute drain time with the cross starting to turn around the 15 minute mark and reaching one rotation every three to four seconds by the end, consistently anticlockwise; and Lloyd Trefethen's five confirming tests in the Southern Hemisphere at the University of Sydney, each settled for 18 hours or more, recording clockwise rotation every time.

videos.description:
It fixed it because, in the summer of 1858, the smell became unbearable, even to the people who ran the country. By the 1850s London held a couple of million people, and roughly half a billion litres of Thames water were drawn back into homes and businesses every day, the very river that carried away the city's sewage.

On 16 June 1858 the temperature in London reached 35 degrees Celsius, the peak of a summer that stayed above 30 degrees for weeks. Blinds in the new Palace of Westminster were soaked in chloride of lime so members could bear to sit inside. The engineer responsible for ventilating the building told the Speaker he could no longer be answerable for the health of the House.

Doctors and MPs believed foul air itself, not water, spread the cholera and typhoid going around that summer. That theory, called miasma, was wrong. But the same stench that frightened Parliament also happened to sit directly over the source of the real, waterborne disease, so a false fear still led to a genuine fix.

Chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works. Chancellor Benjamin Disraeli introduced his sewer funding bill on 15 July 1858, and it became law just eighteen days later, on 2 August.

Length of the new intercepting sewers Bazalgette's team built alongside the Thames, on top of over a thousand miles of smaller street sewers, work that ran from 1859 to 1875.

By 1887, the sewage that had once floated past Parliament had stopped going into the Thames at all.

published the molecular explanation, with Jansa describing the ongoing back and forth between resistant predators and increasingly toxic snakes as a tit for tat evolutionary arms race.

videos.title: Medieval Europe feared it as the Devil's numeral, and the Church banned it outright.
videos.description:
Medieval Europe feared it as the Devil's numeral, and the Church banned it outright. It's in bestselling books. One calls zero 'contraband.' Another says merchants used it in secret, supposedly why the English word for a secret code is cipher.

Oxford's C. Philipp Nothaft found no medieval document that calls zero satanic, and no Church ban on record at all. The trail leads back to a single 1905 article by a philologist, expanded by popular writers from the late 1980s onward.

The city's money-changers' guild, whose surviving statute really does bar members from writing account entries in Hindu-Arabic figures, ordering plain written-out letters instead.

That a 0 could be forged into a 6 or a 9, the reason given in most retellings. The guild's actual 1299 text never says this. It gives no reason at all. The forgery explanation was added by a modern author, in the year 2000.

Even the word cipher isn't a clue. It's just Arabic sifr, zero, spelled the Latin way.

Sources:
- https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:71f4c8ca-2b6a-4393-94dc-8d81096985bc/files/m6bbbf02856bf54fe4b723cdb143485d1: C. Philipp E. Nothaft (All Souls College, Oxford), "Medieval Europe's Satanic Ciphers: On the Genesis of a Modern Myth." Read in full. Establishes that the popular claim is unsubstantiated pseudo-history: the idea that medieval Europe (Church or state) banned zero/Hindu-Arabic numerals as satanic, forcing merchants to use them 'in secret' and supposedly giving English the word cipher for 'code', traces only to a 1905 article by philologist Leo Jordan and expanded from the late 1980s by popular writers (Ifrah, Kaplan, Seife, Teresi, Hitchens, Bellos and others) with no primary-source support. Establishes the one genuine medieval restriction on record: Florence's bankers' guild (Arte del Cambio), Article 102 of its 1299 statute, barred members from recording debits/credits 'by means of the abacus' (Hindu-Arabic style), requiring amounts written out 'openly and in full by way of letters.' The surviving guild text gives no reason and never mentions forgery, fraud, or the Devil; the popular 'a 0 could be forged into a 6 or a 9' explanation is traced to a 2000 book by Midhat Gazalé, with the article noting 'no such comment appears in the source text.' Also establishes the real etymology: Arabic sifr ('zero') was transliterated into Latin as cifra, which became English cipher: a direct transliteration, not evidence of secrecy.

videos.title: Because American TVs refresh at 60Hz, same as the power grid.
videos.description:
Because American TVs refresh at 60Hz, same as the power grid. True in 1941. Not true since 1953.

To fit a new color signal into the same black-and-white broadcasts without interference, the FCC didn't change the picture. It slowed the clock. By exactly one part in a thousand.

The real frame rate NTSC has run at since December 1953, not the clean 30 everyone assumes, and the reason 60fps footage and games have quietly run at 59.94Hz ever since.

A 3.579545 MHz colour signal, tucked in exactly where it wouldn't clash with the old black-and-white one. Millions of existing TVs kept working. Nobody had to buy a new set.

Every '60fps' badge on a game since has been running on a number nobody actually agreed to. It just had to fit around 1953's television sets.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTSC: read in full. Establishes that the original 1941 NTSC black-and-white standard specified 30 frames per second (60 interlaced fields per second) on 525 lines; that in December 1953 the FCC approved a new NTSC colour standard which, to fit a 3.579545 MHz colour subcarrier into the signal without visible interference on the millions of existing black-and-white sets, reduced the frame rate by a factor of 1.001, to 30/1.001 ≈ 29.970 fps (59.94 fields per second); and that the change, about 0.1 percent, was tolerated by existing television sets rather than requiring them to be replaced.

videos.title: Is Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire?
videos.description:
Is Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire? Not close. Oxford had scholars in residence for over three centuries before the Aztec Empire existed at all.

The University's own recorded history: there is no clear founding date, but teaching existed at Oxford in some form by this year.

They didn't reach the Valley of Mexico and found Tenochtitlan, their future capital, until around 1325. That's already 229 years after Oxford had scholars in residence.

In 1428, after a succession crisis tore apart the region's dominant city, Tenochtitlan's ruler Itzcoatl forged a coup with two smaller cities. That alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, known as the Triple Alliance, is what historians call the Aztec Empire.

The gap between Oxford's earliest recorded teaching and the empire most people assume is the older of the two.

Establishes: 'There is no clear date of foundation but teaching existed at Oxford in some form in 1096,' the University's own earliest-recorded-teaching date, well ahead of its listed 1167, 1188 and 1214 milestones.

videos.title: Water is the only substance on Earth that naturally exists as a solid, liquid, and gas.
videos.description:
Water is the only substance on Earth that naturally exists as a solid, liquid, and gas. It's the model answer on the quiz. It is not true.

At its fumaroles, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide gas react and cool into solid yellow crystals. USGS calls it native sulfur, a solid forming right beside the very gases that made it.

Below 115°C, the sulfur stays a solid crystal. Above it, the sulfur melts into vivid orange liquid. Near 200°C the molten sulfur turns red. Past 450°C, with air present, it burns back into gas.

The exact temperature, at a precise 611.657 pascals of pressure, where water itself sits as ice, liquid, and vapour all at once. Real, and comically narrow.

Water isn't unique for doing this. It's just the only one most people ever watch do it.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_point: read in full. Establishes water's triple point (the exact temperature and pressure where ice, liquid water, and vapour coexist) as 273.16 K (0.01°C) at a vapour pressure of 611.657 pascals; this value defined the kelvin until the 2019 SI redefinition and is now an experimentally measured constant instead.
- https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/hvo/news/volcano-watch-many-forms-sulfur-are-found-kilauea-volcano: read in full. USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory article establishing that at Kīlauea's fumaroles (e.g. Sulphur Banks), sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide gas react and cool into native sulfur, a yellow crystalline solid stable below about 115°C; above that temperature it melts into vivid orange liquid; near 200°C molten sulfur turns red; near 450°C with atmospheric oxygen present it burns back into sulfur dioxide gas, all three states occurring naturally and driven by volcanic heat alone.

videos.title: Torvalds did not walk away from BitKeeper. BitKeeper's maker banned him.
videos.description:
Torvalds did not walk away from BitKeeper. BitKeeper's maker banned him.

The Linux kernel began using BitKeeper, a proprietary version control tool, over objections from Richard Stallman and a refusal from veteran developer Alan Cox. BitKeeper's free licence for open source developers forbade them from working on any rival tool, including CVS or Subversion, for as long as they used it.

An OSDL developer working on an unrelated project. His attempt to view BitKeeper's revision history without paying for a licence gave BitMover its reason to end free use.

BitMover did not just shut Tridgell out. It refused to give or sell a licence to anyone employed by OSDL, including Linus Torvalds, who had no part in Tridgell's work. Free use officially ended on 1 July 2005. The Git project began that same year, built to replace BitKeeper for the kernel.

An employee at a company paying for a commercial BitKeeper licence. In October 2005 he agreed to stop contributing to the rival tool Mercurial after BitMover's founder complained.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BitKeeper - read in full: confirms the Linux kernel adopted BitKeeper in 2002 over objections from Richard Stallman and a refusal to use it from veteran developer Alan Cox; that the free licence for open source developers forbade them from working on any rival tool, including CVS, GNU arch, Subversion or ClearCase, for as long as they used it; that BitMover revoked the free version in April 2005, blaming the efforts of Andrew Tridgell, an OSDL developer working on an unrelated project, to view revision metadata the free licence withheld; that BitMover then refused to give or sell a licence to anyone employed by OSDL, including Linus Torvalds and Andrew Morton; that free use officially ended on 1 July 2005; and that in October 2005 BitMover's founder Larry McVoy pressured a paying commercial customer's employee, Bryan O'Sullivan, into agreeing to stop contributing to the rival tool Mercurial.
- https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-A-Short-History-of-Git - Git's own official history page, read in full: confirms the Linux kernel used BitKeeper from 2002, that its free of charge status was revoked in 2005, and that this prompted Torvalds and the kernel community to build their own replacement that same year.

videos.title: It's called the context window, and it isn't really a storage limit.
videos.description:
It's called the context window, and it isn't really a storage limit. It's a cost limit, baked into the maths of how the model reads.

Eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research proposed dropping the older step-by-step reading of text entirely, letting every word compare itself directly against every other word in the sentence at once.

It's also what makes it expensive. Double the text, and the comparisons don't double. They roughly quadruple, and computer scientists have proven this cost can't be dodged, not just observed that it happens.

The fixed context window of every model size in 2020's founding GPT-3 paper: an entire model family sharing the same hard ceiling on how much it could read at once.

Pushing that ceiling higher takes real engineering, not just a bigger number typed into a config file. The comparisons don't get cheaper. Someone still has to pay for all of them.

Sources:
- https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762: read (abstract, metadata and submission history). Establishes 'Attention Is All You Need' as submitted 12 June 2017 by eight authors at Google Brain and Google Research (Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin), proposing the Transformer: a network built solely on attention mechanisms, dropping the recurrence and convolutions of earlier models, explicitly for being 'more parallelizable' since every token can be compared against every other token directly rather than read one step at a time.
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04881: read (abstract). A separate paper proving lower bounds on self-attention's computational complexity, establishing that the time complexity of self-attention is 'necessarily quadratic in the input length' unless the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is false; that is, this is a proven cost, not merely an observed one.
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165: read (abstract and specification detail). 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (GPT-3), Brown et al., OpenAI, submitted 28 May 2020. Establishes that every GPT-3 model size described in the paper uses a fixed context window of n_ctx = 2048 tokens.

videos.title: That number depends entirely on which bits you count.
videos.description:
That number depends entirely on which bits you count. The Computer History Museum's own figure for it is 3.75 megabytes, not 5.

It stored 5 million characters, but each one took 8 bits on the disk, only 6 of those bits were actual data, the rest was parity and spacing. Count all 8 bits per character and you get the famous 5MB. Count only the informational 6, and it's 3.75MB.

Reynold Johnson's team at IBM's San Jose lab built it: fifty 24-inch magnetic disks spinning on a single spindle, the first commercial hard drive.

IBM only leased the whole 305 RAMAC system, disk drive, processor, printer, card punch, all together. The unit weighed over a ton, moved by forklift, occasionally flown in on cargo planes.

The monthly lease for the whole system in 1956, about $36,700 in today's money, and the drive still wasn't yours to keep.

IBM's own engineers said the drive could have held more. Marketing turned it down, they didn't yet know how to sell anyone on wanting more storage than that.

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_305_RAMAC: read. Establishes the system was publicly announced 14 September 1956 (citing a contemporary New York Times article); that the 350 disk unit recorded each of its 5 million characters as 6 data bits plus 1 parity bit plus 1 space bit

videos.title: It paints pixels onto a screen, over and over, very fast.
videos.description:
It paints pixels onto a screen, over and over, very fast. In the early 2000s, researchers found a way to make it do something else entirely: ordinary arithmetic.

So they disguised the maths as a picture. A grid of numbers became a texture. A calculation became a shader painting that texture onto a surface no one would ever actually look at.

Working independently and without knowing about each other, Krüger and Westermann, and separately Bolz, Farmer, Grinspun and Schröder, got graphics chips solving real linear algebra faster than a CPU could, using the same trick, at the same time.

Every calculation still had to be smuggled through a graphics language built for rendering, not maths. Programmers wrote in OpenGL or Direct3D and simply never drew anything with the result.

NVIDIA's answer: a way to write directly for the graphics chip's raw parallel math, released in November, with no disguise required.

Long before AI needed it, the graphics chip had already been tricked into doing sums.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_computing_on_graphics_processing_units: read in full, including cited primary papers. Establishes that general-purpose GPU computing (GPGPU) became practical after 2001, with programmable shaders and floating-point support on graphics chips; cites Larsen & McAllister, 'Fast matrix multiplies using graphics hardware,' presented at the 2001 ACM/IEEE Supercomputing conference, as an early example of GPU-based linear algebra; identifies 2003 as 'a significant milestone,' when two independent research groups, Krüger & Westermann, and separately Bolz, Farmer, Grinspun & Schröder, both in ACM Transactions on Graphics, independently published GPU-based solutions to general linear algebra problems that outran CPUs; establishes that these early efforts required 'reformulating computational problems in terms of graphics primitives, as supported by the two major APIs for graphics processors, OpenGL and Direct3D,' since no general-purpose programming route onto the chip existed yet; and establishes that NVIDIA released CUDA in November 2006, replacing that graphics-disguise workaround with direct general-purpose programming access to the chip.

videos.title: The patent doesn't.
videos.description:
The patent doesn't. Yokoi ran the division that shipped it. He isn't the name on the paperwork.

Nintendo's cross-shaped pad first shipped inside the Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong, credited on the eventual patent to Shirai rather than his better-known boss.

Nintendo filed for it in August 1985 and wasn't granted it until August 1987. Five years after the D-pad had already shipped to shops.

Filed the actual first cross-style four-way controller patent, for Tiger Electronics, it shipped on Tiger's 1980 football handheld as the 'Playmaker' button, two years before Nintendo's version existed.

Not the cross shape, a smaller pad, built for the left thumb, using membrane switches instead of Palisek's bulkier domed ones. That's the whole distinguishing claim, in writing.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad: read. Establishes that Nintendo's cross-shaped D-pad was 'developed by Ichiro Shirai' and first used in the 1982 Game & Watch adaptation of Donkey Kong; that its patented distinguishing features over the earlier Tiger Electronics design were being smaller, positioned for the left thumb, and using membrane switches instead of domed ones; that William F. Palisek patented 'the first true D-pad design for Tiger Electronics' in 1979, debuting on Tiger's 1980 Deluxe Football with Instant Replay handheld as the 'Playmaker' button; and that Nintendo later won a Technology & Engineering Emmy for the design.
- https://patents.google.com/patent/US4687200A/en: read (primary
- https://patents.google.com/patent/US4256931A/en: read (primary). Confirms US4256931A, 'Multiple dome switch assembly having pivotable common actuator,' inventor William F. Palisek, original assignee Interstate Industries Inc (current assignee Tiger Electronics Toys Inc), filed and granted-priority 1979-08-27, published 1981-03-17.
